title: A ceiling on each send
dek: A validated batch limit controls how many jobs leave the queue per send, while the rest wait for later drains.

sections.title: Every pending job left at once
sections.content:
Before this change, a worker tick sent every pending job to the configured /jobs endpoint. The worker called drain(pending), then passed the returned jobs to send. The queue helper used pending.splice(0), which removed all entries from the pending array.

The size of the queue therefore determined the size of the send. With 250 pending jobs, one drain returned all 250 and left the array empty. The shown configuration supplied an endpoint, but no batch-size setting.

sections.title: A growing queue meant a growing batch
sections.content:
You could not set a ceiling on the number of jobs in a send. PR #108 introduces that control with a default of 100. For the same 250-job queue, the first drain should now return 100 jobs and leave 150 queued. With no new arrivals, subsequent drains would return 100 and then 50.

The intended guarantee is a job count, not a memory or processing-time budget. The author explicitly leaves those quantities unbounded by this change. The supplied material motivates a limit on each send; it does not report a measured performance improvement.

sections.title: Configure the count, then retain the remainder
sections.content:
The limit starts in config.ts. The new BATCH_LIMIT environment setting becomes a number, defaults to 100 when absent, and must pass validation during configuration initialization.

{{CODE:0}}

The guard rejects zero, negative numbers, fractions, and values that do not convert to numbers. An invalid setting throws instead of reaching the worker. The default applies to an absent variable; an empty string converts to zero and fails validation.

The central change is in queue.ts: the drain accepts a limit and uses it as the removal count.

{{CODE:1}}

The second argument to splice restricts removal to the first limit entries, or fewer if the queue is shorter. Because the operation changes the original array, the remaining jobs stay queued without a separate requeue step.

The worker connects that operation to the validated configuration in worker.ts.

{{CODE:2}}

Each tick still awaits one send. It passes the configured limit into the drain rather than looping through the entire queue. Together, these three modified files establish the setting, enforce the removal count, and apply it to each send.

Per-tenant scheduling remains outside the change because the queue has no tenant key. The new limit controls batch size across the pending array; it introduces no tenant-aware selection.

sections.title: Send a bounded batch and leave the rest queued
sections.content: PR #108 replaces the all-at-once drain with a configurable job-count limit. The setting defaults to 100 and must be a positive integer at startup. Each worker tick sends at most that many pending jobs, leaving the rest for later drains. The result bounds jobs per send, without claiming a memory ceiling, a time budget, or tenant-aware scheduling.
